items.title: Longest Common Prefix
items.statement: Vertical scan across words stopping at first mismatch.

solutionCode.label: vertical scan: one column at a time across all words

items.complexity: Time O(total characters) worst case, but exits at the first mismatch column. Space O(1).

followups.q: Why anchor on strs[0] rather than the shortest word?
followups.a: The prefix can never be longer than any word, so the loop stops at the first short word via the bounds check anyway. Finding the shortest first costs an extra O(n) pass to save at most a few comparisons — not worth it, but knowing the prefix is bounded by the shortest word is the invariant to state.

followups.q: Why is the bounds check inside the inner loop, not outside?
followups.a: Different words have different lengths, so the check has to be per word per column. Hoisting it out would require pre-computing the minimum length — correct, but it moves work rather than removing it, and the inner check is what makes an empty string in the input return "" immediately.

items.title: String to Integer (atoi)
items.statement: Full rulebook implementation incl. overflow pre-check.

solutionCode.label: strict stage order: whitespace, sign, digits, clamp
solutionCode.py:
INT_MAX, INT_MIN = 2**31 - 1, -2**31

def my_atoi(s: str) -> int:
    i, n = 0, len(s)
    # STAGE 1: leading whitespace only
    while i < n and s[i] == ' ':
        i += 1
    # STAGE 2: at most ONE sign
    sign = 1
    if i < n and s[i] in '+-':
        sign = -1 if s[i] == '-' else 1
        i += 1
    # STAGE 3: digits, clamping rather than wrapping
    result = 0
    while i < n and s[i].isdigit():
        result = result * 10 + int(s[i])
        i += 1
        if sign == 1 and result > INT_MAX:
            return INT_MAX
        if sign == -1 and -result < INT_MIN:
            return INT_MIN
    return sign * result

items.complexity: Time O(n). Space O(1). The stage order is part of the specification, not a style choice.

followups.q: Why is the stage order sacred?
followups.a: Each stage may consume nothing but must not be revisited. "  +-12" reads whitespace, then one sign, then hits '-' which is not a digit — so it returns 0, not −12. Allowing a second sign, or skipping whitespace after the sign, silently changes the answer on exactly the inputs the problem tests.

followups.q: Why clamp instead of letting it wrap?
followups.a: The spec says out-of-range values saturate at INT_MAX / INT_MIN. In C++ signed overflow is also undefined behaviour, so accumulating into an int and checking afterwards is doubly wrong. Accumulate in a wider type and test each step — the check must precede the damage.

items.title: Isomorphic Strings
hints: map<char,char> + set<char> used OR two arrays 256.
Reject when target already used by other source.

solutionCode.label: a bijection needs BOTH directions checked

items.complexity: Time O(n). Space O(1) — two fixed 128-slot tables.

followups.q: Why is a one-directional map wrong?
followups.a: Take "badc" and "baba". Forward gives d→b and c→a with no conflict, so a one-way map accepts it. But b is now the image of both a and d — not a bijection. The reverse map catches it. Any mapping problem phrased as "replace characters" needs the injectivity check.

followups.q: Why does 0 work as the "unmapped" sentinel?
followups.a: Character code 0 is the null character, which does not appear in these inputs. If it could, you would need a separate seen-array or a value of −1 in an int table. Sentinels that collide with real data are a recurring source of subtle bugs — state why yours cannot.

items.title: Reverse Only Letters
hints: Inner skips advance pointers past symbols.

solutionCode.label: two pointers that skip anything that is not a letter

items.complexity: Time O(n). Space O(n) for the result (O(1) if mutating a char array).

followups.q: Why the extra `if (l < r)` before swapping?
followups.a: The two skip loops can leave l == r, or push them past each other, on a string of mostly non-letters. Swapping then is either a no-op or an out-of-order write. The guard is what makes "-" and "a-b-c" behave.

followups.q: How is this the same as Valid Palindrome?
followups.a: Identical skeleton — two pointers with a skip predicate. There the predicate was isalnum and the action was compare; here it is isalpha and the action is swap. Once you see the shape, T205 is the same function with isVowel substituted in.

items.title: Reverse Vowels of a String

solutionCode.label: same skeleton, vowel predicate

items.complexity: Time O(n). Space O(n) for the result.

followups.q: Why must the vowel test be case-insensitive but the swap preserve case?
followups.a: Both 'A' and 'a' are vowels and must participate, but the characters themselves move unchanged — "leetcode" → "leotcede" keeps every letter's original case because you swap the characters, not their lowercase forms. Folding case for the test and not for the move is the distinction.

followups.q: Is 'y' a vowel?
followups.a: Not for this problem — LeetCode 345 lists exactly aeiou in both cases. It is worth asking, because English says "sometimes", and an interviewer who has not pinned it down will accept either as long as you name the assumption.

items.title: String Compression
items.statement: In-place char,count compaction returning new length.
hints: Count run lengths; append digits individually (12 = '1','2').

solutionCode.label: read pointer measures runs, write pointer emits char then digits
solutionCode.py:
def compress(chars: list) -> int:
    write = read = 0
    n = len(chars)
    while read < n:
        c = chars[read]
        run_start = read
        while read < n and chars[read] == c:
            read += 1                       # measure the run
        chars[write] = c
        write += 1
        count = read - run_start
        if count > 1:                       # a run of 1 writes nothing
            for d in str(count):
                chars[write] = d            # 12 becomes '1','2'
                write += 1
    return write

items.complexity: Time O(n). Space O(1) — compaction happens in the input array.

followups.q: Why can the write pointer never overtake the reader?
followups.a: A run of length k is written as 1 character plus at most the digits of k. For k = 1 that is 1 ≤ 1. For k ≥ 2, digits(k) + 1 ≤ k holds for every k (k=2 gives 2≤2, k=10 gives 3≤10). So each run never expands, and write stays at or behind read. That inequality is the whole safety argument for compressing in place.

followups.q: Why write the count digit by digit rather than as a number?
followups.a: The array holds characters, so 12 must become the two characters '1' and '2', not a single value 12. Forgetting this passes on runs under 10 and fails the moment a run reaches double digits — a classic test-case gap.

items.title: Zigzag Conversion
items.statement: Append into numRows buckets bouncing direction.

solutionCode.label: append into row buckets, flipping direction at both rails

items.complexity: Time O(n). Space O(n) for the row buckets.

followups.q: Why does numRows == 1 need a special case?
followups.a: With one row, row is always 0, so it is simultaneously the top and bottom rail. The direction flips to +1 then immediately the bottom test also fires — depending on branch order you either never move or oscillate. The output is just the input, so returning early is both correct and the clearest guard.

followups.q: Why check the top rail before the bottom?
followups.a: For numRows == 2 both conditions can be true on consecutive steps, and with an if/else-if the first match wins. Setting step = 1 at row 0 and −1 at the last row in that order gives the correct alternation. Reversing the order still works for numRows ≥ 3 but is worth tracing rather than assuming.

items.title: Valid Palindrome II (one deletion grace)
hints: On FIRST mismatch try skipping left OR right; verify remainder.

solutionCode.label: branch exactly once at the first mismatch

items.complexity: Time O(n) — one scan, then at most one linear verification. Space O(1).

followups.q: Why is branching only once enough?
followups.a: Everything outside [l, r] already matched, so the deletion must occur inside. At the first mismatch one of the two characters has to go — there is no third option — and after that the budget is spent, so the remainder must be a strict palindrome. Trying to branch again would be spending a second deletion.

followups.q: Why is this O(n) and not O(n²)?
followups.a: The main loop runs at most n/2 times and then returns. The two verification calls are each at most n/2 and only happen once, at the single mismatch. So the total is bounded by about 1.5n — recursion or repeated branching is what would make it quadratic.

items.title: Longest Palindromic Substring
hints: Track bestLo/bestLen on each successful grow.

solutionCode.label: expand from every centre, both parities

items.complexity: Time O(n²) — n centres, each expanding up to n. Space O(1).

followups.q: Why are both centre types mandatory?
followups.a: Odd-length palindromes have a character at the centre ("aba"); even-length ones have a gap ("abba"). Checking only single-character centres misses every even palindrome entirely — "cbbd" would return "c" instead of "bb". It is the most common way this solution is written wrong.

followups.q: Why is the length `r - l - 1`?
followups.a: The while loop exits one step past the valid range on both sides, so the true palindrome spans [l+1, r−1], whose length is (r−1) − (l+1) + 1 = r − l − 1. Deriving it beats guessing; an off-by-one here silently returns a substring one character short.

items.title: Group Anagrams
items.statement: Bucket by sorted-letter key; complexity talk: n·k log k vs count-key n·k.

solutionCode.label: canonical key via a 26-count signature

items.complexity: Sorted-key: O(n · k log k). Count-key: O(n · k). Space O(n · k).

followups.q: Compare the two key designs.
followups.a: Sorting each word costs k log k and yields a short readable key. Counting costs k and yields a fixed-size key. For long words counting wins asymptotically; for k under about 10 the sort has better constants. Say which you would pick and why rather than declaring one universally correct.

followups.q: Why the separator in the count key?
followups.a: Without it, counts of (1, 11) and (11, 1) both stringify to "111" and two different words collide into one group. A delimiter makes the encoding injective — the same reason you cannot concatenate database fields into a composite key without one.

items.title: Integer to Roman / Roman to Integer pair
items.statement: Value-symbol tables both directions; greedy largest-first for encoding.

solutionCode.label: greedy largest-first to encode; subtract-if-smaller to decode

items.complexity: Both O(1) — the loops are bounded by the fixed 13-entry table and by the 15-character maximum roman numeral.

followups.q: Why include CM, CD, XC, XL, IX, IV in the table?
followups.a: Putting the six subtractive forms in the table turns them into ordinary greedy choices — 900 is matched before 500, so 900 never becomes "DCCCC". Handling them as post-hoc string replacements is where implementations get long and buggy. Encode the exceptions as data.

followups.q: Why does greedy produce the canonical numeral?
followups.a: Because the table, with the subtractive pairs included, has the property that each value is more than half the previous one — so taking the largest fitting symbol never forces a worse choice later. That is what makes greedy provably optimal here, unlike arbitrary coin systems where it fails.
